51.correctExplanation: Coarctation distal to the left subclavian artery obstructs flow to the descending aorta, reducing lower-body perfusion and producing an arm–leg pressure gradient.

options.A: This is the keyed decrease: the narrowing reduces perfusion distal to the obstruction, particularly in the legs.
options.B: The upper-body arteries arise proximal to the narrowing, where pressure is preserved or increased rather than selectively reduced.
options.C: Upper-body systolic pressure usually rises proximal to the coarctation; reduced leg pressure is the characteristic contrast.
options.D: The coarctation increases resistance to lower-body flow; it does not remove that obstruction or necessarily reduce distal arteriolar resistance.
options.E: Upper-body vascular resistance is not the defining reduced variable; proximal hypertension and compensatory vascular responses may occur.

52.correctExplanation: Type II pneumocytes synthesize and secrete pulmonary surfactant. Deficiency in premature infants increases alveolar surface tension, promoting collapse and neonatal respiratory distress.

options.A: Capillary endothelial cells form the vascular side of the alveolar barrier; they do not produce alveolar surfactant.
options.B: Bronchial mucous cells produce airway mucus, which is different from the surfactant that stabilizes alveoli.
options.C: The conducting-airway respiratory epithelium clears and conditions inspired air rather than supplying alveolar surfactant.
options.D: Type I pneumocytes form the thin gas-exchange surface; surfactant production is the function of type II cells.
options.E: This is correct: immature type II pneumocytes may not produce enough surfactant to prevent alveolar collapse.

53.correctExplanation: All three conditions can be associated with systemic embolism, although the risks differ substantially. Dilated cardiomyopathy can cause ventricular thrombus, endocarditis can embolize vegetations, and mitral valve prolapse has a much weaker, context-dependent association.

options.A: Dilated cardiomyopathy often produces a large, relatively compliant chamber; decreased compliance is not common to all three diagnoses.
options.B: Depressed systolic contractility characterizes many cardiomyopathies but is not required in uncomplicated mitral valve prolapse or endocarditis.
options.C: Infective endocarditis is infectious, but dilated cardiomyopathy has many noninfectious causes and mitral valve prolapse is usually structural.
options.D: Mitral valve prolapse causes regurgitation rather than stenosis, and neither of the other diagnoses requires mitral stenosis.
options.E: This is the intended shared possibility: intracardiac thrombi or vegetations can embolize systemically. Isolated uncomplicated prolapse does not imply a high embolic risk or a need for anticoagulation.

54.correctExplanation: In left dominance, the circumflex artery supplies the posterior descending artery as well as its usual lateral left ventricular branches. A proximal circumflex occlusion can therefore infarct both the lateral wall and the posterior septum.

options.A: The apex and anterior septum are predominantly supplied by the left anterior descending artery, not the circumflex.
options.B: This combines the circumflex lateral-wall territory with the posterior septal territory supplied through its posterior descending branch in a left-dominant heart.
options.C: Lateral-wall involvement is expected, but this option omits the additional posterior descending territory supplied by the dominant circumflex.
options.D: The posterior septum may be affected, but proximal circumflex occlusion also jeopardizes its lateral left ventricular branches.
options.E: The right ventricular free wall is principally supplied by right coronary branches; it is not the main territory specified by this circumflex occlusion.

55.correctExplanation: Marfan syndrome is usually an autosomal dominant FBN1-related disorder. An affected heterozygous parent has a 50% chance of transmitting the pathogenic variant in each pregnancy, although severity is variable.

options.A: This is correct: each child independently has approximately a one-in-two chance of inheriting the familial pathogenic variant.
options.B: FBN1 variants are identified in most appropriately characterized cases, but a negative molecular test does not exclude every clinically diagnosed case.
options.C: Most affected individuals inherit the disorder; a substantial minority, rather than most, have a de novo variant.
options.D: Many manifestations evolve with growth, making diagnosis more difficult in young children than this statement suggests.
options.E: With a positive family history, diagnostic criteria can be met without two major manifestations; the older major/minor scheme also differs from revised Ghent criteria.

56.correctExplanation: The aortic isthmus just distal to the left subclavian artery is the classic site of blunt deceleration injury, where relatively mobile and fixed segments meet. Treatment timing also depends on associated life-threatening injuries.

options.A: An unstable patient may first need control of another immediately lethal injury; aortic repair is not invariably the first operation in every polytrauma case.
options.B: This is correct: the isthmus near the ligamentum arteriosum is especially vulnerable to deceleration shear.
options.C: Thoracic endovascular aortic repair has an established role and is commonly preferred when anatomy and clinical circumstances permit.
options.D: Repair can use endovascular techniques or selected open approaches; graft interposition is not the only acceptable treatment.
options.E: Distal perfusion during open cross-clamping can reduce spinal cord ischaemia risk compared with unsupported prolonged clamping; saying it has no effect is incorrect.

57.correctExplanation: Ventricular wounds are more frequent than atrial wounds in penetrating cardiac injury, with the anterior right ventricle particularly exposed. Profound hypotension with raised jugular pressure after a precordial stab strongly suggests tamponade requiring urgent operative management.

options.A: Clotted haemopericardium can make pericardiocentesis falsely negative or ineffective; it is not a reliable exclusion test or definitive substitute for surgery in this shocked patient.
options.B: Ventricular wounds are commonly controlled with interrupted, often pledgeted, sutures selected for the injury; a continuous 4-0 repair is not a universal rule.
options.C: Uncontrolled ten-minute inflow occlusion risks severe ischaemia and haemodynamic collapse; any such manoeuvre must be brief and specifically justified.
options.D: This is correct: the ventricles, especially the anterior right ventricle, are injured more often than the atria.
options.E: Carefully placed sutures can repair a wound while preserving an adjacent coronary artery; flow compromise is a risk, not an inevitability.

58.correctExplanation: Postinfarction ventricular septal rupture has very high operative mortality, historically around 30–40% or higher depending on shock, timing and case mix. Definitive treatment must address the rupture while stabilizing perfusion.

options.A: Coronary angiography can inform treatment when feasible, but it should not automatically delay urgent stabilization and repair in a deteriorating patient.
options.B: Mechanical support such as an intra-aortic balloon pump may be introduced early; it is not reserved exclusively for failure of maximal inotropes.
options.C: Anterior infarction with an apical septal rupture is more common overall; posterior defects are associated with inferior infarction.
options.D: The immediately adjacent infarcted edges are friable; repair usually anchors a patch to stronger tissue or excludes the infarct rather than simply sewing to the rupture margin.
options.E: This is the intended historical mortality range. Actual risk can exceed it, especially with cardiogenic shock or emergency early repair.

59.correctExplanation: The great cardiac vein begins as the anterior interventricular vein and travels with the left anterior descending artery in the anterior interventricular groove before entering the coronary sinus.

options.A: This is correct: its anterior interventricular segment directly drains this groove.
options.B: The coronary sinus receives the great cardiac vein but lies mainly in the posterior atrioventricular groove, rather than the anterior interventricular groove.
options.C: The middle cardiac vein accompanies the posterior descending artery in the posterior interventricular groove.
options.D: The small cardiac vein runs mainly along the right cardiac margin and right atrioventricular groove.
options.E: The right marginal vein drains the right margin of the heart, not the anterior interventricular groove.

60.correctExplanation: Primary mediastinal seminoma generally has a better cure rate than mediastinal nonseminomatous germ-cell tumours because of its treatment sensitivity. Modern treatment usually relies on platinum-based systemic therapy, with radiotherapy or surgery used selectively.

options.A: Mature teratoma is a common benign mediastinal germ-cell tumour, so describing teratomas as uncommon is incorrect.
options.B: This is correct: seminomas generally have more favourable treatment outcomes than mediastinal nonseminomatous tumours.
options.C: Pure seminoma does not produce alpha-fetoprotein; an elevated AFP suggests a nonseminomatous component or another cause.
options.D: Nonseminomatous germ-cell tumours are less radiosensitive than seminoma and are primarily treated with chemotherapy, with selected residual-mass surgery.
options.E: Primary resection is not the routine first-line treatment for mediastinal seminoma; systemic therapy is usually central.

61.correctExplanation: The supplied key E needs review: larger CPAM lesions can cause greater lung compression, mediastinal shift or hydrops and are not generally associated with a better prognosis. Large cyst size in a specific histological subtype must not be confused with the overall size of a lung lesion.

options.A: CPAM commonly communicates with the airway to a variable extent, allowing cysts to aerate after birth; absolute noncommunication is not a defining feature.
options.B: Large lesions may impair fetal swallowing and cause polyhydramnios; oligohydramnios is not the characteristic association.
options.C: Air–fluid levels are not specific: congenital diaphragmatic hernia, infection and other cystic lesions can produce similar appearances.
options.D: A symptomatic neonatal lesion commonly needs resection, often lobectomy. However, saying every lesion must be resected without qualification overlooks the debated management of selected asymptomatic lesions.
options.E: This statement conflicts with usual risk assessment: large overall lesion size and hydrops can worsen prognosis. It should not be taught as a general advantage.

61.reviewNote: Key E conflicts with lesion-volume risk; the wording may confuse large-cyst histology with a large lesion. No replacement key assigned. Sources: https://fetus.ucsf.edu/cpam/ ; https://www.chop.edu/conditions-diseases/congenital-cystic-adenomatoid-malformation-ccam

62.correctExplanation: Induction chemotherapy can be used for locally advanced thymoma involving major vessels when an upfront complete resection is unlikely. Resectability and the choice of multimodality treatment require specialist assessment.

options.A: Selected thymomas involving the superior vena cava can be resected with vascular reconstruction; invasion does not make every operation impossible.
options.B: Completely resected stage I thymoma usually has an excellent long-term prognosis, substantially better than the stated 50–60% ten-year survival.
options.C: A typical resectable thymoma can proceed directly to surgery without biopsy; tissue diagnosis is particularly important when nonsurgical treatment or an alternative diagnosis is being considered.
options.D: This is the intended answer for locally advanced disease in which induction treatment may make complete resection feasible; not every limited vessel contact mandates chemotherapy.
options.E: Only a minority of patients with myasthenia gravis have thymoma, usually about 10–15%; the association is often confused with the higher proportion of thymoma patients who have myasthenia.

63.correctExplanation: A Kocher manoeuvre mobilizes the duodenum and pancreatic head, permitting greater cephalad reach of the stomach when additional gastric-conduit length is needed.

options.A: A transhiatal approach avoids thoracotomy but limits direct thoracic exposure and mediastinal lymphadenectomy; those claimed advantages are overstated.
options.B: The gastric conduit is principally based on the right gastroepiploic artery, often with preservation of the right gastric artery; the left gastric artery is usually divided.
options.C: This is correct: duodenal mobilization can reduce tethering and improve the reach of the gastric conduit.
options.D: The abdominal component and conduit preparation commonly precede the right thoracic component of an Ivor Lewis operation; thoracic-first is not obligatory.
options.E: Tumours high above the carina may require a higher resection and cervical anastomosis; an Ivor Lewis intrathoracic anastomosis is not a universal choice for them.

64.correctExplanation: The supplied key identifies fibrinogen, an important adsorbed protein that supports platelet adhesion. However, calling it invariably the first plasma protein to adsorb is problematic: early adsorption depends on the surface, protein concentration and time, and albumin can precede displacement by other proteins.

options.A: Albumin is abundant and can adsorb rapidly at early contact, so it cannot confidently be excluded by a universal claim that fibrinogen is always first.
options.B: Factor VIII is a coagulation cofactor, not the standard dominant first protein coating described in this simplified circuit-contact question.
options.C: Fibrinogen is important in the developing protein layer and platelet adhesion, but the supplied key overstates a surface-dependent adsorption sequence.
options.D: Plasmin is an active fibrinolytic enzyme rather than the typical initial coating protein; circulating plasminogen is its precursor.
options.E: Protein C is an anticoagulant zymogen and is not normally described as the universal first adsorbate on bypass materials.

64.reviewNote: The absolute first-adsorbate claim is oversimplified and may be wrong for the surface described; retain C only as the supplied key pending source review. Protein adsorption/displacement evidence: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8805975/ and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6740550/

65.correctExplanation: For active clinically significant bleeding in HIT, platelet transfusion may be appropriate, making C the intended answer among these products. This is an exception: routine platelet transfusion for HIT-related thrombocytopenia is avoided, and management also requires stopping heparin and specialist selection of non-heparin anticoagulation.

options.A: Cryoprecipitate replaces fibrinogen and selected clotting proteins; it does not specifically replace platelets depleted in HIT unless a separate fibrinogen deficit is documented.
options.B: Fresh frozen plasma supplies coagulation factors but does not directly correct the platelet deficit or the immune platelet activation of HIT.
options.C: This can be appropriate for active significant bleeding, but should not be interpreted as routine treatment of HIT or of an isolated low platelet count.
options.D: Vitamin K reverses vitamin-K antagonist effects; it does not reverse heparin–PF4 antibody-mediated platelet activation.
options.E: Warfarin does not control bleeding and can worsen thrombosis if started before platelet recovery in acute HIT.

66.correctExplanation: Hyperkalaemic cardioplegic arrest greatly reduces myocardial oxygen use by stopping electromechanical work, which is the intended principle behind key C. The alternatives overlap: hypothermia added to arrest further reduces metabolism, so the question needs temperatures and arrest methods to support an absolute ranking.

options.A: An empty beating heart has reduced wall stress but still consumes energy for repeated excitation and contraction.
options.B: A fibrillating heart continues substantial disorganized electrical and mechanical activity, so its oxygen demand remains greater than that of a properly arrested heart.
options.C: This is the intended answer because potassium-induced arrest removes most contractile energy demand; it does not prove superiority over an otherwise equivalent cooled arrested heart.
options.D: Cooling reduces metabolic demand, and a cold arrested heart can consume less oxygen than a warm arrested heart; the unspecified conditions make this option overlap with C.
options.E: Normothermic arrest removes mechanical work but leaves temperature-dependent basal metabolism higher than in a comparable hypothermic arrested heart.

66.reviewNote: The comparison is under-specified: hyperkalaemic arrest can itself be hypothermic or normothermic, and hypothermic arrest includes both arrest and cooling. Preserve C, but do not teach a universal ranking without defined conditions.

67.correctExplanation: Hibernating myocardium is chronically dysfunctional but still viable, adapting to limited perfusion. Restoring blood supply can improve its contraction, unlike established transmural scar.

options.A: An established ventricular aneurysm usually contains scarred, remodelled tissue and is unlikely to recover normal regional contraction simply after revascularization.
options.B: This is correct: viable hibernating muscle has a potential for functional recovery after adequate revascularization.
options.C: Infarcted myocardium has undergone irreversible cell death; dead muscle cannot regain contraction through restored perfusion alone.
options.D: Acute ischaemic dysfunction can also be reversible, but this broad term does not identify the specific chronic viable dysfunctional state tested by the question.
options.E: Akinesis describes absent motion, not tissue viability; an akinetic segment may be hibernating or permanently scarred.

68.correctExplanation: Right dominance is defined by the posterior descending artery arising from the right coronary artery. The supplied option B includes that definition but inaccurately implies that the PDA invariably supplies the AV node; the AV nodal artery usually arises separately near the crux.

options.A: The RCA may give a conus branch regardless of dominance, and the conus artery may also have a separate aortic origin.
options.B: The RCA-to-PDA origin is the defining component, but the added AV nodal claim is anatomically imprecise and should be qualified.
options.C: Posterior septal supply through the PDA is often a consequence of right dominance, making this broadly true as well; arterial origin, rather than territory alone, defines dominance.
options.D: The sinoatrial nodal artery can arise from either the RCA or circumflex and does not define posterior coronary dominance.
options.E: Dominance is not determined by a percentage of right ventricular supply; it is determined by the origin of the PDA.

68.reviewNote: Key B contains an imprecise AV-node clause, while C is also generally true in right dominance. No new key assigned; distinguish PDA origin from the separate AV nodal artery.

69.correctExplanation: Postinfarction septal rupture accompanies extensive myocardial damage, so survivors have a greater tendency to ventricular aneurysm formation than survivors of uncomplicated infarction.

options.A: Complex or serpiginous basal ruptures are more associated with inferior infarction; anterior LAD infarcts more often cause a simpler apical septal defect.
options.B: Septal rupture usually follows a transmural infarct; a predominantly subendocardial infarct does not commonly destroy the full septal thickness.
options.C: This is correct: the extent of myocardial injury underlying the rupture also predisposes to ventricular aneurysm.
options.D: Early outcome is driven especially by shock, ventricular function and haemodynamic instability, rather than coronary disease extent alone.
options.E: Mitral regurgitation can coexist, particularly with inferior infarction, but functional mitral insufficiency in two-thirds of all rupture patients is not a reliable general rule.

70.correctExplanation: A persistently perfused false lumen after repair of aortic dissection can promote distal enlargement and later aortic events. This explains key B, but the stem incorrectly treats this as a feature of every thoracic aneurysm.

options.A: Hypertension is also an adverse aortic risk factor and requires treatment, so it is not intrinsically a harmless comparison; false-lumen status is the intended dissection-specific predictor.
options.B: This is the intended answer after dissection repair: continued false-lumen flow can maintain wall stress and permit later aneurysmal expansion.
options.C: A thin aneurysmal wall can be concerning, but its visual thickness is not the standard postoperative predictor targeted by the false-lumen options.
options.D: Complete false-lumen thrombosis is generally more favourable than continued patency, although partial thrombosis and individual anatomy need separate assessment.
options.E: Early discharge usually reflects an uncomplicated recovery; by itself it is not a pathological predictor of later aortic enlargement.

70.reviewNote: False lumens are features of dissection, not of all thoracic aneurysms. The stem needs a dissection context, and hypertension is also adverse; preserve the supplied B without implying A is universally false.

71.correctExplanation: Across aortic dissections, a common primary entry-tear site is the proximal ascending aorta, a short distance above the aortic valve. The descending isthmus is another important site, particularly in type B dissection.

options.A: This is a common site for descending/type B tears and traumatic injury, but not the overall answer intended when all dissections are considered.
options.B: This is correct: the proximal ascending aorta is a frequent primary entry site in the common type A pattern.
options.C: Arch tears occur but are less typical overall than tears in the proximal ascending aorta.
options.D: Primary distal descending tears can occur but are not the most common overall site.
options.E: The area just proximal to the left subclavian origin is not the characteristic dominant primary entry location across all aortic dissections.

72.correctExplanation: No valid replacement key is assigned. In this context dP/dt means the rate of change of pressure with time, conventionally left ventricular pressure when assessing ventricular contractility; fibre shortening is a different quantity.

options.A: This option describes left atrial pressure change, whereas the intended cardiac contractility measure is left ventricular pressure change; it is not an unambiguous replacement for the defective source key.
options.B: Cardiac index is flow normalized to body surface area; its rate of change is not dP/dt.
options.C: Fibre lengthening is a mechanical length-change measure, not a pressure derivative.
options.D: Relaxation is related to negative ventricular dP/dt and other measurements, but it is not the complete definition of dP/dt.
options.E: Fibre shortening is not the definition of the pressure derivative, even though contraction can produce a pressure rise.

72.reviewNote: The existing unresolved status is preserved. The correct pressure/time definition is not accurately stated by an unambiguous option; do not assign or narrate a replacement letter.

73.correctExplanation: A tiny, stable iatrogenic descending-aortic intimal injury can often be managed conservatively with monitoring and blood-pressure control. However, observation means a structured assessment with imaging and surveillance, not ignoring an uncharacterized aortic injury.

options.A: Continuing an elective coronary procedure without assessing the new aortic injury risks extension and is not an appropriate automatic next step.
options.B: Immediate open repair is generally disproportionate for a confirmed limited, asymptomatic descending injury without rupture, progression or malperfusion.
options.C: Cross-sectional imaging can be important to define extent and complications, so it cannot be dismissed if the lesion has not already been adequately characterized.
options.D: This is the intended management strategy for a verified small uncomplicated injury, provided close monitoring, appropriate imaging and haemodynamic management are included.
options.E: Emergency endovascular repair is normally reserved for complications or a concerning injury pattern, rather than every tiny stable intimal flap.

73.reviewNote: Key D is reasonable only after adequate characterization; the stem does not establish the extent of injury. Do not teach unqualified observation instead of assessment, imaging and surveillance.

74.correctExplanation: Chronic pulmonary regurgitation is common after historical TOF repairs involving a transannular patch. Long-standing right ventricular volume overload can cause dilatation, exercise limitation and arrhythmias in adult life.

options.A: A residual or recurrent VSD can cause symptoms, but it is not the characteristic most common late problem after an otherwise complete TOF repair.
options.B: Branch pulmonary artery stenosis may persist and requires surveillance, but chronic pulmonary regurgitation is the classic frequent late lesion.
options.C: Residual pulmonary stenosis is possible, but historical relief of outflow obstruction often produces the opposite problem: pulmonary insufficiency.
options.D: This is correct: important pulmonary regurgitation can progressively enlarge and impair the right ventricle.
options.E: Aortic regurgitation can occur with aortic-root disease in repaired TOF, but it is not the usual leading explanation in this comparison.

75.correctExplanation: An unexpectedly highly oxygenated sample from an umbilical venous catheter can suggest infracardiac anomalous pulmonary venous drainage into the portal or hepatic venous system. This is a clue requiring echocardiographic confirmation and verification of catheter position, not a diagnosis from oxygen content alone.

options.A: Transposition can produce severe cyanosis and mixing abnormalities, but does not characteristically direct oxygenated pulmonary venous blood into the hepatic/umbilical venous pathway.
options.B: An unusual arterial–venous fistula could also oxygenate local venous blood, but this is not the classic anomalous pulmonary venous drainage mechanism intended by the stem.
options.C: An ordinary ASD or VSD does not directly connect pulmonary venous return to the hepatic venous system sampled by the catheter.
options.D: This is the intended clue, particularly for infracardiac pulmonary venous return draining toward the portal/hepatic veins.
options.E: Supplemental oxygen can alter measured blood oxygen levels, but it does not explain a selective, disproportionately oxygenated umbilical venous sample in the same anatomical way.

76.correctExplanation: A persistent left superior vena cava commonly drains into the coronary sinus. It can therefore cause a markedly enlarged coronary sinus with continuing systemic venous return even during ordinary right-sided bicaval cannulation.

options.A: Partial anomalous pulmonary venous drainage usually enters a systemic vein or right atrium through another route; it does not best explain the classic combination of a very large coronary sinus and heavy return through it.
options.B: This is correct: a left SVC entering the coronary sinus creates an additional venous return pathway that standard bicaval drainage may miss.
options.C: An unroofed coronary sinus can cause interatrial communication and may coexist with a left SVC, but the stated findings alone most directly suggest the persistent left SVC.
options.D: An ASD permits interatrial flow but does not itself account for a greatly dilated coronary sinus with return emerging from its ostium.
options.E: Poor caval drainage causes blood to collect through the caval orifices; it does not specifically explain disproportionate return through an enlarged coronary sinus.

77.correctExplanation: The intended key C appears to investigate a cardiac source or right-to-left shunt allowing catheter-associated venous thrombus to cause paradoxical arterial embolism. However, a newly cold leg requires urgent limb-viability assessment and vascular management; echocardiography must not delay limb-saving treatment.

options.A: Arterial imaging can locate the obstruction and guide treatment if it does not delay urgent revascularization, so this is not categorically wrong for an acutely ischaemic leg.
options.B: Routine cardiac catheterization is not the initial test for catheter-associated thromboembolism or the immediate management of acute leg ischaemia.
options.C: Echocardiography can look for a cardiac embolic source or shunt, but the stem omits the findings needed to make it the universally best immediate test.
options.D: A septic screen can be appropriate if infection is suspected, but it does not assess arterial perfusion or promptly locate an embolic source.
options.E: Venography can assess venous thrombosis, but a cold ischaemic leg suggests arterial compromise and requires urgent vascular evaluation.

77.reviewNote: The supplied key is not safely generalizable from this incomplete emergency stem; limb viability and urgent vascular treatment take priority. Guidance: https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.02.013

78.correctExplanation: In the classic heterotopic transplant arrangement, a donor pulmonary-artery extension with prosthetic conduit may be needed to bridge the distance to the recipient pulmonary artery while retaining the native heart.

options.A: The donor aorta can usually be connected to the recipient aorta directly; a prosthetic aortic conduit is not the characteristic requirement being tested.
options.B: This is the intended answer: the pulmonary artery connection may need an interposition graft because of its position and limited reach.
options.C: Atrial connections are fashioned between atrial tissues rather than routinely requiring a prosthetic graft.
options.D: The operation does not normally depend on prosthetic reconstruction of the recipient inferior vena cava as described here.
options.E: Superior caval/atrial anastomotic arrangements vary, but the pulmonary artery extension is the classic prosthetic connection in this question.

79.correctExplanation: With the coronary sinus used as the retrograde inflow route, Thebesian venous channels can provide drainage directly into the cardiac chambers. Retrograde flow also exits through coronary arterial ostia and other venous communications, so drainage is not identical to ordinary antegrade coronary circulation.

options.A: Anterior cardiac veins drain mainly the right ventricular surface directly into the right atrium, but they are not the principal generalized route intended here.
options.B: The great cardinal vein is an embryological structure, not an adult myocardial venous drainage route for this technique.
options.C: The SVC returns systemic venous blood to the right atrium; it is not a direct myocardial microvenous drainage pathway.
options.D: This is correct in the intended retrograde-perfusion context: Thebesian channels open directly from myocardium into cardiac chambers.
options.E: The coronary sinus is delivering the retrograde cardioplegia through the catheter, so it is functioning as inflow rather than the ordinary venous outflow route.

80.correctExplanation: Completely calcium-free perfusion can predispose to the calcium paradox: reintroducing calcium during reperfusion can cause severe membrane injury and calcium overload. Controlled calcium content is therefore important.

options.A: This is correct: the absence of calcium can set up calcium-paradox injury when calcium is reintroduced.
options.B: Magnesium can help limit calcium entry and support cardioplegia, but its absence is not the classic calcium-paradox mechanism tested here.
options.C: Manganese is not a standard essential component whose omission defines this cardioplegia reperfusion injury.
options.D: Potassium is important for depolarizing cardioplegic arrest, but the question targets injury after calcium-free exposure and calcium reintroduction.
options.E: Sodium concentration affects ionic balance and cell volume, but its absence is not the named calcium-paradox mechanism.

81.correctExplanation: An elevated left hemidiaphragm after PDA surgery suggests left phrenic nerve injury. If the child remains successfully extubated and clinically stable, observation is appropriate because recovery can occur; significant respiratory compromise may require plication.

options.A: Plication is useful for symptomatic diaphragmatic paralysis or failure to wean ventilation, but it is not automatically required in a stable extubated three-year-old.
options.B: Reintubation is indicated for respiratory failure, not an isolated radiographic elevation in a child who is breathing adequately.
options.C: Phrenic nerve stimulation is not routine initial treatment for an acute presumed surgical phrenic injury in this setting.
options.D: This is correct for the clinically stable child described: monitor respiratory status and allow time for possible nerve recovery.
options.E: Nerve grafting is not standard immediate management for this postoperative finding and cannot be justified by the radiograph alone.

82.correctExplanation: The right ventricle may become stiff or dysfunctional after TOF repair because of prior hypertrophy, ischaemia, ventriculotomy and altered loading. This is a common important contributor to postoperative low cardiac output.

options.A: Left ventricular dysfunction can occur, but the right ventricle is the chamber directly affected by the outflow reconstruction and pre-existing pressure load.
options.B: A significant residual VSD can impair haemodynamics, but a VSD is intended to be closed and is not the usual general explanation after a technically satisfactory repair.
options.C: This is correct: right ventricular dysfunction or restrictive physiology can limit forward output after repair.
options.D: Mitral regurgitation is not a usual intrinsic component of TOF or its repair and is a less likely general cause.
options.E: Coronary injury is a serious possible cause, particularly with unusual coronary anatomy, but it is not the most common explanation across routine repairs.

83.correctExplanation: Desaturated effluent from the right coronary ostium during retrograde cardioplegia raises concern about inadequate right-coronary territory protection or venous admixture. Supplementing with direct antegrade ostial cardioplegia improves delivery to myocardium that retrograde flow may protect poorly.

options.A: This is correct: direct antegrade ostial delivery can supplement the incompletely protected right ventricular territory.
options.B: The problem may be distribution rather than the oxygen content of the prepared solution; simply increasing oxygen does not ensure right ventricular delivery.
options.C: More retrograde volume may still bypass poorly perfused regions and is not a reliable correction of the distribution problem.
options.D: Excessive coronary sinus pressure risks venous injury and oedema without guaranteeing adequate right ventricular perfusion.
options.E: Moving the catheter into the right atrium would lose selective coronary sinus infusion and worsen delivery rather than improve myocardial protection.

84.correctExplanation: Combined valve and coronary bypass surgery generally carries greater perioperative stroke risk than an isolated routine procedure because patients and operations tend to have greater vascular burden, complexity and aortic manipulation.

options.A: This is the intended comparison: combined operations commonly have a higher observed stroke rate than isolated CABG or routine isolated valve surgery.
options.B: Isolated valve surgery carries stroke risk, but combined valve/CABG often adds coronary disease, operative duration and manipulation.
options.C: Isolated CABG carries embolic and hypoperfusion risk, but the combined operation generally has a higher-risk profile.
options.D: Double-valve surgery is also complex and may carry substantial risk; the exact ranking depends on the population, although the supplied key favours combined valve/CABG.
options.E: MIDCAB often avoids cardiopulmonary bypass and extensive ascending-aortic manipulation, reducing these particular contributors to stroke.

85.correctExplanation: Aortic cannulation can dislodge atheromatous material and cause cerebral embolism, which explains the supplied key A. However, side-clamping and other aortic manipulations are also major embolic triggers, and no universal highest-risk step can be assigned without aortic pathology and procedural context.

options.A: This is the keyed embolic mechanism: cannulation of a diseased ascending aorta can release plaque into the cerebral circulation.
options.B: Side-biting clamps can also dislodge aortic plaque and generate emboli, so this is a genuine risk rather than a categorically safe alternative.
options.C: Ventricular manipulation can impair haemodynamics or contribute to air/debris embolism, but direct manipulation of an atherosclerotic aorta is the intended mechanism.
options.D: Retrograde cannula placement is not normally a direct source of aortic atheroembolism, although any cardiac instrumentation has possible complications.
options.E: Axillary cannulation is sometimes chosen to avoid a diseased ascending aorta; its neurological risk depends on anatomy and technique rather than being inherently the highest.

85.reviewNote: The absolute highest-risk ranking between aortic cannulation and side-clamping is not established by this stem; preserve A as the source answer but qualify the competing aortic embolic risks.

86.correctExplanation: After the earliest technical/thrombotic phase, intimal hyperplasia is the characteristic process narrowing saphenous vein grafts during the first postoperative year. Later failure increasingly involves accelerated atherosclerosis.

options.A: Atherosclerosis becomes a more prominent mechanism later; it is not the characteristic early months-to-one-year process in this comparison.
options.B: This is correct: smooth-muscle proliferation and extracellular-matrix accumulation thicken the graft intima after exposure to arterial pressure and injury.
options.C: Technical errors tend to cause very early failure, often through poor flow or thrombosis, rather than the characteristic progressive narrowing over the first year.
options.D: Persistent spasm is not the usual dominant cause of months-long saphenous vein graft narrowing.
options.E: Progression in the native proximal coronary artery does not itself produce structural narrowing within the vein graft.

87.correctExplanation: Emergency redo CABG combines the hazards of re-entry and difficult anatomy with haemodynamic instability and little time for optimization. This makes emergency status a particularly strong adverse factor among the listed choices.

options.A: Female sex can be associated with risk differences in some cohorts, but emergency redo surgery is generally a more powerful immediate adverse circumstance.
options.B: Advanced age increases operative risk, but age alone is not the strongest factor in the intended comparison with an emergency reoperation.
options.C: Poor left ventricular function is important, but the urgency and instability of emergency surgery add major risk beyond an isolated risk factor.
options.D: This is correct: emergency status often means unstable ischaemia or collapse, limited preparation and a more difficult rescue operation.
options.E: COPD increases pulmonary complications, but it is not the strongest overall predictor among these choices in the intended redo-CABG comparison.

88.correctExplanation: The Ross operation requires work close to coronary anatomy and reimplantation of the coronary arteries. Coronary injury, distortion or impaired perfusion can produce myocardial ischaemia and ventricular arrhythmias after surgery.

options.A: Inadequate myocardial protection can cause arrhythmias, but the operation-specific concern emphasized here is coronary injury or compromised coronary flow.
options.B: A paravalvular leak does not characteristically explain frequent early ventricular arrhythmias without evidence of a major haemodynamic consequence.
options.C: This is the intended answer: damage, tension or kinking involving a coronary vessel can cause ischaemia-driven ventricular arrhythmias.
options.D: Right ventricular trauma may contribute to arrhythmias, but it does not identify the more important coronary-perfusion complication of the Ross procedure.
options.E: Pulmonary regurgitation can have long-term right ventricular effects, but it is not the best explanation for frequent immediate postoperative ventricular arrhythmias.

89.correctExplanation: Severe aortic stenosis creates a fixed outflow obstruction with dependence on adequate preload, vascular resistance and coronary perfusion. Anaesthetic-induced hypotension can therefore precipitate profound ischaemia or arrest.

options.A: Aortic regurgitation has different loading requirements and does not produce the same classic fixed-output response to induction-related vasodilation.
options.B: Severe mitral stenosis is anaesthetically hazardous, but critical aortic stenosis is the classic lesion associated with collapse from loss of vascular resistance and coronary perfusion.
options.C: This is the intended answer: a severely stenotic aortic valve limits the ability to increase cardiac output when anaesthesia lowers blood pressure.
options.D: Mitral regurgitation can cause heart failure, but modest afterload reduction may improve forward flow; it is not the classic fixed-outflow mechanism.
options.E: Mixed aortic disease may include severe stenosis and be high risk, but the isolated physiological lesion specifically tested is aortic stenosis.

90.correctExplanation: Persistent bleeding after difficult mitral replacement raises concern for a surgical source, including atrioventricular-groove injury, and may require prompt re-exploration. However, the stated drainage rate and unspecified coagulopathy do not by themselves establish that immediate reoperation is always the best next step.

options.A: This is the supplied answer if a significant surgical bleed or tamponade is suspected; treatment should not be delayed in a deteriorating patient.
options.B: A subxiphoid window would not adequately identify and repair many postoperative surgical bleeding sources, particularly a potential mitral annular or ventricular injury.
options.C: Cryoprecipitate is appropriate for a demonstrated fibrinogen deficit, but an unspecified abnormal coagulation profile does not prove that deficit.
options.D: TOE can clarify tamponade or a structural complication when transthoracic windows are poor and may be useful if the patient is stable enough; it should not delay necessary re-exploration.
options.E: Platelets should be guided by platelet count/function and the clinical situation; previous FFP administration does not establish that platelet transfusion is the missing intervention.

90.reviewNote: Management is under-specified: 100 mL/hour for six hours with abnormal coagulation is not an automatic re-exploration threshold without haemodynamic status or suspected surgical source. Retain A as supplied, with urgent individualized evaluation. Guidance: https://www.aats.org/tsra-primer-post-operative-bleeding

91.correctExplanation: New inferior-wall dysfunction while failing to separate from bypass suggests inadequate right-coronary territory perfusion. Assessing and correcting a failed or inadequate RCA graft addresses the suspected cause; the associated mitral regurgitation may be ischaemic.

options.A: Moderate ischaemic mitral regurgitation can improve when regional perfusion is restored; valve repair should not precede evaluation of the suspected graft problem automatically.
options.B: Mitral replacement does not correct the likely inferior-wall ischaemia and adds major intervention without first addressing the probable cause.
options.C: An intra-aortic balloon pump can support perfusion and unloading, but it does not repair an occluded or inadequate coronary graft.
options.D: This is the intended answer if assessment confirms graft failure or inadequate flow: restore effective right-coronary perfusion rather than treating its consequences alone.
options.E: Adrenaline may support haemodynamics temporarily but increases oxygen demand and cannot correct a mechanical graft obstruction.

92.correctExplanation: Postoperative junctional ectopic tachycardia is an automatic tachycardia. Controlled cooling is one accepted way to reduce its rate and restore haemodynamic coordination, alongside electrolyte correction, reduced catecholamine drive and selected antiarrhythmic treatment.

options.A: Beta blockade may be used selectively, but it is not the characteristic primary manoeuvre tested for this postoperative automatic junctional rhythm.
options.B: Verapamil can cause severe hypotension and cardiovascular collapse in infants and is not an appropriate routine treatment for postoperative infant JET.
options.C: Hypokalaemia should be corrected, but giving potassium without a documented deficit does not reliably terminate JET and can be dangerous.
options.D: This is the intended answer: carefully controlled cooling suppresses automaticity and can help control the rhythm; treatment often requires several measures rather than cooling alone.
options.E: Bretylium is not standard treatment for postoperative junctional ectopic tachycardia.

93.correctExplanation: A subarterial VSD can permit aortic cusp prolapse and progressive regurgitation. Closing the VSD when regurgitation is still mild may remove the mechanism driving further valve damage; valve intervention depends on the actual cusp anatomy and residual regurgitation.

options.A: This is the intended answer: close the defect before aortic cusp damage progresses, with intraoperative reassessment of valve competence.
options.B: Aortic valve repair may be necessary with significant cusp distortion or persistent important regurgitation, but it is not automatically required for every mild leak.
options.C: Valve replacement is disproportionate for mild regurgitation when the native valve may remain competent after VSD closure.
options.D: A Ross procedure is not the routine response to a VSD-associated mild aortic leak and exposes the patient to unnecessary additional valve surgery.
options.E: Observation alone risks progressive cusp prolapse and regurgitation in this subarterial defect; delaying closure is not the intended strategy.

94.correctExplanation: In partial AV septal defect repair, the conduction tissue lies close to the inferior septal margin. Routing the patch suture line to leave the coronary sinus on the left atrial side can avoid injury to the displaced AV node and conduction axis.

options.A: The purpose is not to decompress the right atrium; coronary venous drainage normally enters the right atrium without a need for such relief.
options.B: Ease of suturing is secondary; protection of the abnormal conduction-tissue position is the important anatomical reason.
options.C: A correctly constructed right-sided coronary sinus can remain patent; occlusion is not inevitable simply because it is left on the usual atrial side.
options.D: This is correct: avoiding sutures near the conduction system reduces the risk of postoperative AV block.
options.E: The right coronary artery is not the structure determining this atrial patch route; the concern is the AV node and conduction axis.

95.correctExplanation: An unroofed coronary sinus communicates with the left atrium. Coronary or associated left-SVC venous return can therefore enter the left atrial operative field despite drainage of the usual superior and inferior caval veins.

options.A: Uncontrolled systemic venous return is a possible general mechanism, but an unroofed coronary sinus provides the specific abnormal pathway into the left atrium intended here.
options.B: This is correct: absence of part of the coronary sinus roof opens a venous channel directly into the left atrium.
options.C: A second ASD creates an interatrial communication, but it does not by itself explain continuing venous inflow into the left atrium when caval drainage is adequate.
options.D: Complete absence of the coronary sinus is not the usual specific lesion producing the described left atrial inflow; an unroofed sinus is the classic association.
options.E: A persistent ductus venosus connects portal and systemic venous circulations and does not directly account for this left atrial surgical-field flooding.

96.correctExplanation: TOF with markedly dilated pulmonary arteries suggests the absent pulmonary valve variant. Dilated branch pulmonary arteries can compress the trachea and main bronchi, causing severe respiratory distress.

options.A: A vascular ring can compress the airway, but the stated aneurysmal pulmonary arteries themselves provide the relevant compressive mechanism.
options.B: This is the intended answer: tracheobronchial compression by the enlarged pulmonary arteries causes major airway obstruction.
options.C: The large VSD contributes to TOF physiology but does not mechanically compress the airway in the way described.
options.D: Right ventricular hypertrophy reflects pressure loading; it is not the direct cause of compression by dilated branch pulmonary arteries.
options.E: Pulmonary stenosis contributes to the cardiac lesion but does not itself explain the airway compression from the enlarged pulmonary arteries.

97.correctExplanation: Persistent clear, low-triglyceride drainage after a prosthetic modified BT shunt can reflect plasma leakage through the graft rather than chylothorax. The source key proposes replacing it with a contralateral classic shunt, but the stem does not specify a prosthetic graft or establish that this particular operation is required.

options.A: This is the intended definitive way to remove a leaking prosthetic shunt while maintaining pulmonary blood flow through a native-vessel connection, if that anatomy and diagnosis are confirmed.
options.B: Drainage may remove accumulated fluid but does not eliminate ongoing leakage from a porous graft.
options.C: Simply removing a necessary shunt can critically reduce pulmonary blood flow; another adequate source must be secured.
options.D: Revision or replacement can be appropriate depending on the precise shunt defect and anatomy, so this broad alternative cannot be excluded without more operative detail.
options.E: TPN is used in selected chylothorax management, but triglyceride-free plasma-like fluid suggests a different mechanism; in a fasting child, fluid testing still needs careful interpretation.

97.reviewNote: The intended mechanism assumes a prosthetic modified BT shunt, but the stem only says BT shunt. Confirm graft type and serous leakage before treating A as a universal next operation; no replacement key assigned.

98.correctExplanation: Balloon angioplasty is a well-established treatment for suitable discrete recurrent coarctation, particularly in children, and can avoid a difficult redo operation. The best intervention nevertheless depends on age, anatomy, aneurysm risk and prior repair; adults often undergo stenting.

options.A: This is the intended answer for an anatomically suitable recurrent narrowing, especially in paediatric practice.
options.B: Redo surgery remains appropriate for selected complex anatomy, long-segment narrowing or associated aneurysm; it is not invariably inferior to catheter treatment.
options.C: An extra-anatomical bypass can be used in selected complex situations, but an axillary–femoral bypass is not the routine first treatment for a simple recurrent arch narrowing.
options.D: A subclavian flap is a surgical reconstruction option, but repeat anatomy and previous repairs may limit it and it is not the general first catheter-based choice.
options.E: Blood-pressure therapy is important but does not remove a haemodynamically significant mechanical obstruction that requires intervention.

98.reviewNote: The unqualified best-treatment statement needs age/anatomy context; contemporary adult management commonly uses stenting or surgery. Retain A as the source key. Guidance: https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2022.08.004

99.correctExplanation: Abciximab inhibits platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors and can markedly increase bleeding risk during urgent cardiac surgery. Having platelets available provides haemostatic support if significant bleeding or platelet dysfunction requires transfusion.

options.A: Aprotinin is an antifibrinolytic; it does not replace or directly restore platelets inhibited by abciximab.
options.B: Additional red-cell cross-matching may be needed according to bleeding risk, but a fixed ten-unit order does not specifically address the platelet defect.
options.C: This is correct: platelets should be available because of potent recent antiplatelet exposure; actual transfusion depends on bleeding and haemostatic assessment.
options.D: Cryoprecipitate mainly addresses fibrinogen deficiency, not direct IIb/IIIa receptor blockade.
options.E: Fibrinogen replacement can help a measured fibrinogen deficit but does not specifically correct the drug-induced platelet inhibition.

100.correctExplanation: A patent in-situ LIMA graft to the circumflex usually lies toward the left lateral pericardium rather than directly beneath the sternum. In this anatomical comparison it is less exposed at re-entry than enlarged anterior structures or an anterior right-coronary vein graft.

options.A: A patent RCA vein graft may lie anteriorly close to the sternum and can be injured during re-entry, causing severe bleeding or ischaemia.
options.B: An enlarged right ventricle can adhere directly behind the sternum and is vulnerable to laceration during sawing and dissection.
options.C: This is the intended exception: a left-sided LIMA-to-circumflex course is generally away from the median re-entry plane, although preoperative imaging and individual anatomy still matter.
options.D: Right atrial enlargement can bring the atrium into a more exposed anterior/right parasternal position, increasing injury risk.
options.E: A markedly enlarged ascending aorta can lie close to the posterior sternum, making re-entry injury potentially catastrophic.
